lessons.title: Common Moat Analysis Mistakes: A Final Checklist

body.text: Almost every mistake in moat analysis is one of three things: calling something a moat that is not, missing that a real moat is shrinking, or paying a price that leaves nothing for you even when you were right.

children.text: Seven chapters, twenty-six lessons, and it comes down to a short list of recurring errors. This closing lesson collects them, gives you the fix for each, and leaves you with a single page you can work through for any company on the NSE or BSE.

body.caption: Calling something a moat when it is not

cells: Treating a good business as a protected one
Name which of the five sources applies. If you cannot, there is no moat
Chapter 1
Assuming a famous brand means pricing power
Check whether gross margins held through inflation and whether prices rose with volumes intact
Chapter 2
Counting market share, first-mover status, growth, or a brilliant CEO as a moat
Apply the ₹10,000 crore test and the leadership test
Chapter 1
Believing a regulatory licence is automatically scarce
Count how many competitors hold the same licence. Dozens means it is a ticket to compete, not protection
Chapter 2
Accepting network effect claims on user or GMV numbers
Test the take rate, contribution margin, and marketing spend as a share of revenue
Chapter 3
Ignoring multi-homing
Ask whether users and suppliers are also active on rival platforms
Chapter 3
Judging on one year of ROCE, or on the average alone
Use the ten-year median, the minimum, and the count of years above the hurdle
Chapter 5
Mistaking formula-linked cost pass-through for pricing power
Check whether margins expand when input costs fall, and check customer concentration
Chapter 5
Ignoring incremental ROCE
Compare the change in EBIT with the change in capital employed over five years
Chapter 5
Assuming profit equals cash
Compare five-year operating cash flow with five-year net profit, and watch debtor and inventory days
Chapter 5

body.caption: Getting the direction or the price wrong

cells: Scoring the level of a moat but not its direction
Track leading indicators: the volume and price split, incremental ROCE, and share in the growing channel
Chapter 6
Paying any price for quality, then anchoring to your purchase price
Work backwards from the price to the implied growth, and judge every future decision from today, not from your cost
Chapter 7

body.text: Look at where the mistakes cluster. Six are about identification, four about measurement, and two about judgement. But the two judgement errors cause the largest losses, because they occur after you have done all the analysis correctly and feel most confident.

body.title: Final Recall: The Course in Twelve Cards

cards.definition: A structural advantage that keeps returns above the cost of capital despite competition. Not execution, not fame, not size.
Intangible assets, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages, and efficient scale.
ROCE sustained above the cost of capital across a full cycle, with a respectable worst year.
What could a well-funded rival not replicate within five years? If the answer is nothing much, there is no moat.
Price increases that stick while volumes hold, and gross margins that recover within a few quarters of a cost shock.
Users active on several platforms at once. It is the main reason marketplace network effects fail.
A market too small to support a second player profitably. It weakens as the market grows.
Change in EBIT ÷ change in capital employed. It reveals moat erosion years before reported ROCE does.
Five-year operating cash flow ÷ five-year net profit. Profit rising while cash stays flat is a red flag.
Direction, not level. Gaining share without cutting prices is the most reliable sign of widening.
(1 − g ÷ ROIC) ÷ (r − g). High returns make growth cheaper, which is why moats deserve a premium.
Wide moat, narrowing trend, premium valuation. Every backward-looking number supports the thesis while the forward-looking ones do not.

children.text: This is the whole course as a sequence. Work through it in order, because each step can stop the process.

body.title: The Final Moat Checklist
steps: Name the moat source. If you cannot name one of the five, stop here
Check that customers behave accordingly: prices stick, churn is low, or users concentrate
Apply the ₹10,000 crore test. If money could replicate it in five years, stop here
Pull ten years of ROCE from Screener.in: median, minimum, years above 15%, and the trend
Check margin stability through FY22 and FY23, and separate pricing power from cost pass-through
Compare five-year operating cash flow with five-year net profit
Calculate incremental ROCE and compare it with reported ROCE
Score durability: trend, regulatory and technology exposure, and the reinvestment runway
Total the 24-point scorecard and write one line of evidence for every score
Work backwards from the share price to the growth it implies, and ask whether your evidence supports it
Set position size from the gap between implied assumptions and evidence, not from conviction
Write down the two or three indicators that would change your mind, and the date you will check them

children.text: Each quarter, twenty minutes per holding:
read the results presentation for the volume and price split, any discounting, and commentary on competition. Update your leading indicators.
Once a year, after the annual report:
rescore the full twelve criteria, compare with last year including the reasons, and note which criteria moved.
rescore immediately after a regulatory consultation, a large acquisition, a funded new entrant, or a technology announcement.
rescore because the share price moved. Price movement is not evidence about the moat, and rescoring in reaction to it is how investors talk themselves into or out of positions.

Twelve holdings at twenty minutes a quarter is about four hours a quarter. That is the realistic time cost of investing directly using this framework. If that is more than you want to spend, the fund routes in the previous lesson exist for exactly that reason.

body.title: Final Check: Put It All Together
body.question: A company has a 10-year median ROCE of 27%, a minimum of 22%, cash conversion of 94%, and a clear switching cost moat. Its incremental ROCE over five years is 11%, volumes have been flat for two years with growth entirely price-led, and it trades at 58 times earnings. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: A wide moat at a fair price, given the excellent historical numbers
A wide moat that is narrowing, at a price that assumes it is widening: the most dangerous combination
No moat, because incremental ROCE is low
A cash cow that should be valued on its dividend stream
body.explanation: The historical evidence is excellent and the moat source is clear, so this is a genuine wide moat. But incremental ROCE of 11% against a 27% median, flat volumes, and price-led growth are three independent signs of narrowing. At 58 times earnings, the price assumes sustained high growth. Strong past, weakening present, demanding price: exactly the combination Chapter 6.4 warned about.

body.title: The Last Principle
body.textWithBlank: Identifying a moat correctly tells you about the business. Your return also depends on the ___ you pay and how long the moat lasts.
body.explanation: The whole course reduces to this: a durable advantage, bought at a price that does not already assume more than the advantage can deliver.

body.title: Your First Real Analysis
body.scenario: You have finished the course and want to apply it. You own six stocks and three mutual funds. Two of the stocks you bought on a friend's recommendation years ago and have never analysed. One has tripled, one has halved. You have about three hours this weekend.
body.prompt: How would you spend those three hours to get the most value from this framework?
body.modelAnswer: Start with the two unanalysed stocks, and treat the price history as irrelevant, because a tripling tells you nothing about whether a moat exists and a halving does not mean there is none. Spend roughly forty minutes on each: name the moat source, apply the ₹10,000 crore test, pull ten years of ROCE from Screener.in for the median, minimum and trend, and check incremental ROCE against reported ROCE. That alone will tell you whether you own a protected business or a lucky one. Spend the next forty minutes on the overlap check across your three funds: list the top ten holdings of each and see how much duplication exists, and whether the moat businesses you own directly are also large positions in your funds, which would mean far more concentration than you think. Use the final forty minutes to write down, for each of the six stocks, one sentence naming the moat source and one sentence stating what would make you sell. Those twelve sentences are worth more than any amount of further reading, because they are what you will check against reality next year. What not to do with the three hours: score all six companies in exhaustive detail, run valuation models on every one, or make any trade this weekend. The framework works through repetition over years, not through one intense session.

body.label: Where the edge actually comes from
body.value: Not from spotting moats, which many investors can do, but from judging direction and price, which most do not
body.context: The scorecard, the trend indicators, and the implied growth calculation are the three habits that separate the two.

body.text: This course is educational material, not investment advice. All companies mentioned across the course were used to illustrate concepts from public information, and all worked examples use hypothetical figures. Market conditions, regulations, and company circumstances change. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.

points: Most errors fall into three groups: misidentifying a moat, missing that it is narrowing, and overpaying for a real one
Six identification errors, four measurement errors, and two judgement errors cover almost everything that goes wrong
The two judgement errors cost the most, because they happen after the analysis is done and confidence is highest
Work the checklist in order: source, customer behaviour, the ₹10,000 crore test, then the numbers, then durability, then price
Write one line of evidence for every score and two or three indicators that would change your mind
Rescore quarterly on leading indicators and annually in full, but never because the share price moved
